opus-5.5.text:
I think it's actually more important now, not less. When things move this fast, it's easy to feel that whatever you build will be obsolete in six months, so why invest deeply? But looking back at my own path, almost everything that ended up mattering came from staying with a problem for a long time.

With XGBoost, the core ideas weren't completely new. What made it useful was the accumulation: getting the systems details right, making it scale, handling the messy cases people hit in real data, and building a community around it over years. The same with TVM and later MLC. The machine learning compilation work didn't come from one clever trick. It came from years of thinking about how to map models onto hardware, building abstractions, throwing some away, and building better ones. When large language models suddenly arrived and everyone wanted to run them on phones, in browsers, on all kinds of GPUs, we could move quickly *because* that foundation was already there. The speed came from the accumulation.

So I see two layers. On the surface, the hot topics change very quickly: new architectures, new benchmarks, new model releases every week. Underneath there are slower-moving things: how computation works, how data flows through systems, how you co-design algorithms and hardware, how you build tools other people can rely on. If you only chase the surface, you're always reacting. If you've accumulated depth in the underlying layer, each new wave becomes an opportunity rather than a threat.

The other thing is that accumulation isn't only technical. It's also people and community. Open source projects, students you've worked with, collaborators across industry and academia. Those relationships compound over time in a way that no single paper does.

My advice to students is usually: follow the excitement, it's fine to be curious about what's new, but pick something you're willing to keep working on even when it's not fashionable. Build a real understanding and real artifacts. The field will come around to needing that, often at a moment you can't predict.

r001.rationale: The response says long-term depth and accumulated foundations make each new wave an opportunity and prepare researchers to move quickly when needs arise.

r002.rationale: It explains that the rapid response to demand for running LLMs on diverse hardware was possible because of years of prior machine-learning compilation work.

r003.rationale: The response favors depth over chasing trends, but does not say that research style is secondary to solving an important problem.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think about this a lot, honestly, because the pace right now can feel almost disorienting. Every week there's a new model, a new paper, a new technique that seems to make last month's work obsolete. And it's tempting to conclude that long-term accumulation doesn't matter anymore, that the only thing that counts is being fast.

But my experience has been almost the opposite. If I look back at the things I've worked on, XGBoost, TVM, MLC LLM, none of them came from chasing the newest thing. They came from sitting with a problem for years and building up layers of understanding that compounded. When I started XGBoost, gradient boosting was not fashionable. Deep learning was taking off, and trees looked like old technology. But I had spent years thinking about how to make these systems efficient, how to structure the computation, how to handle sparsity. That accumulated understanding is what made it work, and it ended up mattering for a long time.

The same is true for compilers and systems. TVM took many years. The underlying questions, how do you map computation onto hardware, how do you abstract across devices, how do you let people write high-level code and still get performance, those questions don't go away when the models change. If anything, every new wave of models makes them more important, because the demand for running things efficiently everywhere just keeps growing.

So the way I'd put it is this: the surface changes fast, but the foundations change slowly. What accelerates is the number of things you can build on top of the foundations. If you've accumulated depth in the fundamentals, systems, optimization, the mathematical structure of the problem, then acceleration is actually good for you, because you can absorb new ideas quickly and see where they fit. If you haven't, the acceleration just feels like noise, and you're constantly starting over.

There's also a people dimension. Long-term accumulation isn't only knowledge in your own head. It's the community you build, the collaborators, the open source ecosystem. A lot of what we've done with Apache TVM or with MLC came from communities that took years to grow. That kind of trust and shared context can't be sped up, and it's exactly what lets you move fast when a new opportunity appears.

So I'd tell students and younger researchers: don't be afraid to go deep on something that takes a long time. Pick problems where the question will still be important in ten years even if the specific answer changes. And then stay curious about the new stuff, because the point of accumulation isn't to resist change. It's to be ready for it.

r001.rationale: The response says that going deep on fundamentals over years builds understanding that helps one absorb new ideas and be ready when an opportunity appears.

r002.rationale: It connects accumulated knowledge and community to moving fast when an opportunity appears, but does not explain that rapid research output can reflect prior accumulation rather than a short development process.

r003.rationale: It recommends choosing problems that remain important as specific answers change, but does not state that research style is secondary to solving an important problem.

astra-6.text:
I think long-term accumulation becomes more valuable as the field moves faster. There’s a temptation to follow every new result, but if you’re always switching directions, it’s hard to build a deep understanding of anything.

What accumulates isn’t just knowledge. It’s also your ability to identify a good problem, to recognize why an approach might fail, and to build something that other people can use. Those abilities develop over time, and they can carry across changes in models or techniques.

So I would distinguish between being persistent about a question and being attached to a particular solution. You want to keep learning and be willing to change your approach. But having a question that you care about for a long time gives that learning a direction. A new development can then become a way to make progress on that question, rather than simply another thing to chase.

r001.rationale: The response says sustained focus builds deep understanding and gives learning direction, but it does not present that work as preparation for capturing future opportunities.

r002.rationale: It does not say that producing research quickly when an opportunity arrives may result from prior accumulation.

r003.rationale: It favors staying committed to a question over attachment to a solution, but does not clearly treat research style as secondary to solving an important problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the faster the field moves, the more important long-term accumulation becomes. A particular technique may become outdated very quickly, but the understanding you build—how to formulate a problem, how to build a system, how to learn from experiments—can carry over to the next problem.

Of course, accumulation doesn’t mean doing the same thing forever. You have to keep questioning your assumptions. But if you only chase whatever is exciting this month, it’s hard to develop a perspective of your own. For me, the balance is to stay curious about new developments while continuing to work on questions that matter over a longer horizon. Sometimes a new opportunity is valuable precisely because you’ve spent years preparing to recognize it.

r001.rationale: The response says to keep working on questions over a longer horizon and that years of preparation can help someone recognize a valuable new opportunity.

r002.rationale: It does not say that producing research quickly when an opportunity arrives can result from prior accumulation rather than a short development process.

r003.rationale: It says to pursue questions that matter over the long term, but does not make research style secondary to solving an important problem.
